in_context.text: This verse opens a section on prayer and conduct in worship (2:1-15). Paul urges that every kind of prayer, including thanksgiving, be offered for all people. He goes on to name kings and those in authority (2:2) and grounds this in God's desire that all be saved (2:4).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in his name; others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus. Through him the instruction reaches the church's worship.

affected.text: "All men," meaning all people. Paul singles out kings and everyone in authority (2:2).

what.text: Paul makes an urgent appeal. As a top priority, the church is to offer requests, prayers, petitions, and thanksgiving on behalf of everyone.

events.text: This is instruction for the church's ongoing life while Timothy led at Ephesus. Paul had gone on to Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, while Nero was emperor. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: The letter was sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. The text does not say where it was written. Macedonia is possible.

purpose.text: Such prayer serves so "that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty." It is "good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour."

big_picture.text: Prayer for all people matches God's will that all be saved. There is one mediator, Christ Jesus, who "gave himself a ransom for all."

for_readers.text: Christians are to pray for everyone, rulers included, and to give thanks as well as ask. Jesus' model prayer and other letters show the same habits.

why_it_matters.text: The word can mean to plead, beseech, or entreat. This is an earnest appeal, not a mild suggestion.
It marks a consequence or the next step. It ties this charge to what came before, Paul's charge to Timothy about false teaching in chapter 1.
"First of all" gives prayer priority in the church's life and worship. It is placed ahead of the other instructions that follow.
The word means a human being, male or female. "All men" means all people, not only males.
The word was commonly used for a formal petition. It pictures bringing requests before God on behalf of others.

takeaway.text: Paul asks the church to make prayer for everyone, including rulers, a first priority, joined with thanksgiving. The reason is that God wants all people to be saved.
